content: I want to build an app to save and manage bookmarks.

Built a polished, responsive bookmark manager called **Markwell**.

Features include:

- Add and delete bookmarks
- Search across titles, domains, descriptions, and tags
- Favorites and read-later filtering
- Collections with live counts
- Grid and list layouts
- Sorting controls
- Persistent browser storage
- Responsive desktop/mobile interface
- Empty states, action menus, and notifications

The production build succeeds and core flows were browser-tested.

Review it at **http://maker:4000**

Key files: [App](/work/src/main.jsx) · [Styles](/work/src/styles.css) · [Package configuration](/work/package.json)

This looks really polished — the library view is clear and easy to read, and I can see everything's organized nicely.

Before I can say it's what I need, though, the one thing I most want to see is the actual saving part in action. Everything you've shown me is the browsing view with links already in it. The whole point for me is: I find a page I like, I paste its link in, and it gets saved so I can come back to it later.

Two things I'd want to check on that:

1. Can you walk me through adding a brand-new bookmark — I click "Add bookmark," put in a link, and it shows up in my library?
2. When I paste a link, does it pull in the page's title and a short description on its own? I really don't want to type all that out by hand every time — grabbing those details automatically is a big part of why I want this.

Could you show me that flow?

content:
Yes—the full save flow now works at **http://maker:4000**:

1. Click **Add bookmark**.
2. Paste a URL.
3. Markwell automatically retrieves the page title and description.
4. Review or edit the detected details.
5. Click **Save bookmark**.
6. The new bookmark appears first in **All bookmarks** and persists locally.

I tested it with an MDN page. It automatically found “JavaScript | MDN” and its full description, then created the ninth bookmark.

Screenshots:

- [Automatic metadata preview](/work/prototypes/add-bookmark-preview.png)
- [Bookmark saved in the library](/work/prototypes/bookmark-saved.png)

Some websites block automated metadata requests. When that happens, Markwell explains the issue but still allows the URL to be saved with manually editable details.

That's exactly what I was hoping for. Pasting a link and having it pull in the title and description on its own — with a chance to look them over and tweak before saving — is the heart of what I wanted. And I like that if a site blocks it, you still let me save the link and fill in the details myself rather than just failing.

(Side note: the two screenshots you linked didn't open on my end, and the live view still shows the original 8. But your description of the flow covers my concern well, so I'm satisfied the saving works.)

This part's good for me. Let's keep going.

content:
Great. The live view showing eight is expected: my test ran in an isolated browser session, while your browser has its own local storage.

The strongest next step is replacing browser-only storage with real accounts and cloud persistence, so bookmarks survive across devices. After that, I’d prioritize duplicate detection, import/export, and a browser-extension-friendly quick-save endpoint.

Tell me which direction you want next, and I’ll build it.

Honestly, the cloud accounts and cross-device syncing aren't a priority for me — this is just for my own use, and saving locally is fine for now. Same with the browser extension; I can live without it.

What matters more to me is getting good at organizing and finding what I've saved. A few things I'd care about:

- **Tags** — being able to put tags on a bookmark and then click a tag to see just those. That's how I'd actually keep things sorted.
- **Not ending up with duplicates** — if I save a link I already saved before, I'd rather it take me to edit the existing one than pile up a second copy.
- **Bringing in the bookmarks I already have** — I've got a pile in my browser already, so being able to import them (and export back out) would matter.

Of those, tagging and filtering by tag is the one I'd start with — it's the most useful to me day to day. Let's go that way next.

content:
Tagging and filtering are now live at **http://maker:4000**.

You can now:

- Click any tag on a bookmark to filter the library immediately.
- Use the tag bar and overflow menu to browse all tags.
- See bookmark counts beside each tag.
- Open a bookmark’s `•••` menu and choose **Edit details & tags**.
- Add comma-separated tags; new tags automatically become filters.
- Clear the filter with **All**.

I verified adding a new “Essential” tag to an existing bookmark and filtering down to that single result. The production build passes with no browser-console errors.

This is what I wanted. I can see the tags with their counts along the top, click one to narrow down to just those bookmarks, and add or change tags from a bookmark's menu. That covers how I'd keep things organized — good.

For what's next, let's do the "don't pile up duplicates" piece: if I try to save a link I've already saved, take me to edit the existing one instead of making a second copy.

content:
Duplicate prevention is now live.

When you paste an existing link, Markwell:

- Recognizes equivalent URLs despite `www`, trailing slashes, fragments, or common tracking parameters.
- Opens the existing bookmark’s edit dialog.
- Lets you update its title, description, collection, or tags.
- Keeps the library count unchanged.

I tested an altered tracked version of `increment.com`: Markwell opened the original “The craft of writing software” bookmark, saved its edits, and retained exactly eight bookmarks. New URLs continue through the normal metadata-and-save flow.

That's exactly right — saving a link I already have takes me to the existing one to update instead of making a second copy, and the count stays put. Even handles the messy tracking-parameter versions, which is a nice touch. Good.

Next, let's do the import/export piece — bringing in the bookmarks I already have saved in my browser, and being able to export them back out.

content:
Import and export are now available from **Import & export** in the lower-left menu.

Import:

- Accepts standard HTML exports from Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari.
- Preserves browser folders as collections and filterable tags.
- Retains tags already stored in the export.
- Skips duplicate and tracking-parameter variants.
- Reports how many bookmarks were imported or skipped.

Export:

- Downloads every bookmark as a dated, browser-compatible HTML file.
- Preserves titles, URLs, descriptions, collections, and tags.

I verified the round trip with two new bookmarks and one duplicate: Markwell imported two, skipped the duplicate, then exported all ten bookmarks successfully.

That completes my whole wishlist. Bringing in my existing browser bookmarks — folders becoming collections and tags, duplicates skipped, and a clear count of what came in — is just what I needed, and being able to export everything back out means I'm never locked in. 

Stepping back: saving a link with the details filled in for me, organizing with tags, searching, favorites and read-later, no duplicate pile-ups, and now import/export — that's everything I set out to be able to do with my bookmarks, and it all holds together. I'm happy with it as it stands.
